title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: "Varvara Andreevna, when I was very young I set up in my mind the ideal of the woman I would love and be happy to call my wife. I have lived a long life, and now, for the first time, I have met what I was looking for — in you. I love you, and I offer you my hand."
Sergey Ivanovitch was saying this to himself as he closed the last ten paces between him and Varvara. She was kneeling, hands held over the mushrooms to keep Grisha off them, calling little Masha.
"Come over here, little ones! There are so many!" she was saying in her sweet, deep voice.
Seeing Sergey Ivanovitch coming up, she didn't stand or change her position, but everything about her told him she felt his presence and was glad of it.
"Well, did you find any?" she asked from under the white kerchief, turning her handsome, softly smiling face to him.
"Not one," Sergey Ivanovitch said. "Did you?"
She didn't answer; the children were swarming around her.

"That one too, near the twig," she pointed out to little Masha — a small mushroom split across its rosy cap by a dry stalk of grass it had pushed up through. Varenka got up while Masha picked it, breaking it into two white halves. "This takes me back to my childhood," she added, moving away from the children to Sergey Ivanovitch's side.

They walked on for a few steps in silence. Varenka could see that he wanted to speak; she could guess about what, and felt faint with joy and panic. They had walked far enough that no one could hear them now, but still he didn't start. It would have been better if Varenka had stayed silent. After a stretch of silence it would have been easier to say what they wanted to say than after talking about mushrooms. But against her own will, as if by accident, Varenka said:

"So you didn't find anything? Though there are always fewer in the middle of the wood." Sergey Ivanovitch sighed and didn't answer. He was annoyed that she had brought up mushrooms again. He wanted to circle her back to those first words about her childhood; but after a long pause, as though against his own will, he made a remark in response to her last words.
"I've heard the white edible funguses are mostly found at the edge of the wood, though I can't tell them apart."

A few more minutes passed; they moved still further from the children and were quite alone. Varenka's heart was pounding so hard she could hear it, and she felt herself turning red, then pale, then red again.

To be the wife of a man like Koznishev, after her time with Madame Stahl, struck her imagination as the height of happiness. On top of that, she was almost sure she was in love with him. And it had to be decided in the next minute. She was frightened. She dreaded both his speaking and his not speaking.

Now or never the thing had to be said — Sergey Ivanovitch felt that too. Everything in Varenka's expression — the flushed cheeks, the lowered eyes — betrayed an agonizing suspense. Sergey Ivanovitch saw it and felt sorry for her. He even felt that to say nothing now would be an insult to her. Quickly, in his head, he ran through all the arguments for his decision. He even went over the words in which he meant to put his proposal — but instead of those words, some entirely unexpected thought that drifted into his head made him ask:
"What's the difference between a 'birch' mushroom and a 'white' mushroom?"
Varenka's lips trembled as she answered:
"In the cap there's hardly any difference — it's in the stalk."

And the instant the words were out, both of them felt that it was over, that what was supposed to be said would not be said; and the emotion that had been mounting in them up until then began to subside.
"The stalk of a birch mushroom looks like a dark man's chin after two days without shaving," Sergey Ivanovitch said, now speaking quite calmly.

"Yes, that's true," Varenka answered with a smile, and without realizing it they had changed direction. They were beginning to head back toward the children. Varenka felt sore and ashamed; at the same time she was relieved.
Once he was home again and went back over the whole thing, Sergey Ivanovitch decided his earlier resolution had been a mistake. He couldn't be unfaithful to Marie's memory.
"Gently, children, gently!" Levin shouted, almost angrily, at the children, planting himself in front of his wife to shield her as the pack came flying toward them with shrieks of delight.

Behind the children Sergey Ivanovitch and Varenka came out of the wood. Kitty didn't need to ask Varenka anything; from the calm, somewhat crestfallen faces of the two of them she could see that her plan had not come off.
"Well?" her husband asked her as they were heading home.
"It doesn't bite," Kitty said, her smile and her way of speaking recalling her father — a likeness Levin often noticed with pleasure.
"How doesn't it bite?"
"Like this," she said, taking her husband's hand, lifting it to her mouth, and just barely brushing it with closed lips. "Like a kiss on a priest's hand."
"Which side didn't it bite on?" he asked, laughing.
"Both sides. But it should have been like this...."
"There are peasants coming...."
"Oh, they didn't see."
